subChunks.title: Container Queries
subChunks.hookHtml: Responsive design with viewport breakpoints has one fundamental weakness: a component's layout depends on the screen width, not its own container width. A card that should be horizontal when it's 500px wide — whether that's in a full-screen layout or a narrow sidebar — can't achieve this with sm: breakpoints. Container queries solve this by making components respond to their own container's size.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem with viewport breakpoints for components

/* This card goes horizontal at 640px VIEWPORT width */
<div class="flex flex-col sm:flex-row gap-4">

/* Problem: if this card is in a 300px sidebar on a 1200px screen,
   the sm: breakpoint still fires and makes it horizontal — which
   doesn't fit the sidebar at all. */

Container query syntax in Tailwind v4

In Tailwind v4, container queries are built-in using @container. You create a containment context and then use @sm:, @md:, @lg: variants on children to respond to the container's width, not the viewport.

/* 1. Mark the container */
<div class="@container">

  /* 2. Respond to the container's width */
  <div class="flex flex-col @sm:flex-row gap-4">
    <img class="w-full @sm:w-32 @sm:h-32 object-cover rounded-lg" />
    <div class="flex-1">
      <h3 class="font-semibold text-gray-900">Card Title</h3>
      <p class="text-sm text-gray-500">Description</p>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>

Container query breakpoints

@xs:    /* ≥ 320px container width */
@sm:    /* ≥ 384px container width */
@md:    /* ≥ 448px container width */
@lg:    /* ≥ 512px container width */
@xl:    /* ≥ 576px container width */
@2xl:   /* ≥ 672px container width */

These breakpoints are relative to the container, not the viewport. The same component will display differently depending on how wide its wrapping @container element is.

Named containers

/* For nested containers, name them to avoid ambiguity */
<div class="@container/card">
  <div class="@lg/card:flex-row">...</div>
</div>

Real-world use case — the adaptive card

/* This card adjusts its own layout based on how much space it has */
<div class="@container">
  <article class="flex flex-col @md:flex-row gap-4 bg-white rounded-xl p-4">

    <!-- Image: full width stacked, or square thumbnail side-by-side -->
    <div class="aspect-video @md:aspect-square @md:w-32 @md:flex-none overflow-hidden rounded-lg">
      <img class="w-full h-full object-cover" src="..." />
    </div>

    <div class="flex-1">
      <h3 class="font-semibold text-gray-900">Quest Name</h3>
      <p class="text-sm text-gray-500 mt-1 @md:line-clamp-2">Description</p>
      <!-- Show XP only when there's enough room -->
      <p class="hidden @lg:block text-sm font-medium text-blue-600 mt-2">500 XP</p>
    </div>
  </article>
</div>

When to use container queries vs viewport breakpoints

  • Use viewport breakpoints (sm:, md:) for page-level layout decisions — overall page structure, navigation patterns.
  • Use container queries (@sm:, @md:) for component-level layout decisions — cards, list items, widgets that can appear in different contexts.

Maester Cordell: "Container queries are the single biggest improvement to responsive CSS in a decade. A component that adapts to its own space — not the viewport — is a truly reusable component. Place it in a full-width layout or a narrow sidebar and it handles itself. That is what component-first design actually means."

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: A component that changes layout based on the viewport is not truly reusable. Put it in a sidebar and it still thinks it is full-screen. Container queries break this dependency — the component adapts to its own allocated space, wherever it appears. This is the future of responsive design.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build an adaptive quest card that switches from stacked to horizontal layout based on its container width:

  • .card-container: @container
  • .quest-card: flex, flex-col, @md:flex-row, gap-4, bg-white, rounded-xl, border, border-gray-100, overflow-hidden
  • .quest-image: aspect-video, @md:aspect-square, @md:w-36, @md:flex-none, overflow-hidden
  • .quest-image img: w-full, h-full, object-cover
  • .quest-info: flex-1, p-4
  • .quest-xp: hidden, @lg:block, text-sm, font-medium, text-blue-600, mt-2

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a component library card that uses container queries to show three different layouts: stacked (narrow, < 384px), horizontal with thumbnail (medium, 384px-512px), and full horizontal with extra metadata visible (wide, > 512px). Place the same component in both a full-width container and a narrow sidebar container to verify it adapts correctly. No starter code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the fundamental difference between viewport breakpoints (sm:, md:) and container queries (@sm:, @md:). Give a concrete example of a component that would break with viewport breakpoints but work correctly with container queries. What does @container do, and what is a named container (@container/name) useful for?

questions.prompt: Which class marks an element as a container query context in Tailwind v4?
questions.explanation: @container applies the CSS containment context (container-type: inline-size) to the element. Children of this element can then use @sm:, @md:, @lg: variants to respond to the container's width rather than the viewport width.

questions.prompt: A card component uses @md:flex-row to switch to horizontal layout at 448px container width. When this card appears in a sidebar that's only 280px wide, what happens to the layout?
options: It stays in the default flex-col (stacked) layout — @md: checks the container width, not the viewport, and 280px is below the 448px threshold
It switches to flex-row because the viewport is wider than 448px
It breaks the layout — container queries don't work inside narrow containers
It uses the viewport width as a fallback
questions.answer: It stays in the default flex-col (stacked) layout — @md: checks the container width, not the viewport, and 280px is below the 448px threshold
questions.explanation: This is exactly the power of container queries. The @md: variant activates at 448px of the nearest @container's width. Since the sidebar is 280px wide (its @container element is 280px), @md: doesn't activate and the card stays stacked. If this same card were placed in a 600px column, @md: would activate and it would go horizontal.

questions.prompt: You're building a dashboard with a main column (70% width) and a sidebar column (30% width). Both columns render the same quest card component. You want the card to be horizontal in the main column and stacked in the sidebar. Which approach is correct?
options: Wrap each card in a @container div and use @md:flex-row on the card — it will automatically be horizontal in the wide column and stacked in the narrow one
Use md:flex-row viewport breakpoints on the card — it will adapt to the overall page width
Pass a prop to the card component that manually sets the layout variant
Container queries don't work inside CSS grid columns — use JavaScript to detect column width
questions.answer: Wrap each card in a @container div and use @md:flex-row on the card — it will automatically be horizontal in the wide column and stacked in the narrow one
questions.explanation: This is the exact use case container queries were designed for. Wrapping each card placement in a @container div makes the card respond to its own allocated space. In the 70% column (likely > 448px), @md:flex-row activates. In the 30% column (likely < 448px), it doesn't — the card stays stacked. No JavaScript or prop passing needed.
